sources.title: Human History Map historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Exact repository record checked: nan-chao is a circa state record dated 800 to 1279 and remains distinct from the separate nan-zhao predecessor record dated 700 to 800.

sources.title: Human History Map world-700 topology
sources.note: Decoded predecessor seam. The exact nan-chao id is absent; a separate nan-zhao feature is present and is not aliased to this card.

sources.title: Human History Map world-800 topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one 20-position Polygon that omits Taihe, Dali and Weishan, includes Kunming and Luang Prabang, and is therefore seriously misplaced southeast of the historical core.

sources.title: Human History Map world-900 topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one 21-position Polygon with the same misplaced southeastern footprint just before the historical Nanzhao dynasty ended in 902.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1000 topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one 12-position Polygon shifted west to include Dali, Weishan and Kunming during the successor Dali kingdom rather than historical Nanzhao.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1100 topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one 12-position Polygon continuing the west-shifted footprint during the Later Dali kingdom, after the brief Dazhong interruption.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1200 topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one 14-position Polygon with a footprint similar to 1100, representing an atlas label that outlived the historical Nanzhao state.

sources.title: Human History Map world-1279 topology
sources.note: Decoded ending seam. The exact id is absent, so 1279 is an imported atlas cutoff and not the fall date of either Nanzhao or Dali.

sources.title: Dali Prefectural Government: history of the Sui and Tang periods
sources.note: Official regional historical account used only for the overview: Erhai unification, capitals, the 902 overthrow, short successor regimes and the founding of Dali in 937.

sources.title: Academy of Chinese Studies: Nanzhao Culture
sources.note: Educational cultural-history synthesis used narrowly for the historical Nanzhao span ending in 902 and the continuity of regional culture beyond one ruling house.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of China: Nanzhao Kingdom, 649 to 902
sources.note: Publisher encyclopedia synthesis used for Nanzhao diplomacy, Tang and Tibetan alliances, military expansion and the kingdom’s status as a major southwestern power.

sources.title: Yunnan Provincial Library: The Nanzhao Dehua Stele
sources.note: Provincial-library account of the 766 court inscription, its political purpose, later weathering and the earlier copies through which more of its text survives.

sources.title: Chun Xu: Reaping the Benefits of Water
sources.note: Heidelberg dissertation, especially printed pages 120 and 123, used for Erhai rice cultivation, channels, embankments and the transmitted Chinese text and translation of the Dehua inscription.

sources.title: Wuzhishan Nanzhao temple excavation report
sources.note: Xinhua report quoting excavation director Zhu Zhonghua on courtyard buildings, Buddhist finds, pottery kilns, firing tools, rejects and the tile inscribed guanjia sheli.

sources.title: Yunnan Provincial Archaeology Institute field report on Wuzhishan
sources.note: Regional publication of the provincial institute field report, used for split-level halls, stone foundations and courtyard drainage; it does not identify a toilet or wastewater sewer.

sources.title: Fan Chuo: Man shu, bilingual annotated edition
sources.note: Ninth-century Tang outsider’s account, checked against the Chinese on printed page 100, for women’s clothing, servants and courtship music made with gourds and leaves.

sources.title: Chinese Text Project: Man shu, volume seven on products
sources.note: Searchable primary-text edition used for one annual paddy harvest followed by winter barley and for the management of salt wells; treated as the same underlying work as other Fan Chuo evidence.

sources.title: State Ethnic Affairs Commission: historical source for a Nanzhao feast
sources.note: Official article reproducing Fan Chuo’s passage about eleventh-lunar-month brewing, cattle, sheep and visits among relatives and neighbors; used as medieval evidence, not timeless custom.

sources.title: Shao-yun Yang: Sun Qiao and Nanzhao in Chengdu
sources.note: Scholarly sourcebook introduction used for elite Nanzhao youths studying literacy and numeracy in Chengdu and for the 829 capture of artisans and silk weavers.

sources.title: Megan Bryson: Southwestern Chan in texts and art
sources.note: Peer-reviewed study used for the 899 Illustrated History of Nanzhao, Buddhist royal foundation stories, the end of Nanzhao and the establishment of Dali in 937.

sources.title: Megan Bryson: Buddhist Kingship in Tenth-Century Dali
sources.note: Asia Major article abstract and publication record used for Nanzhao’s fall, the Changhe regime from 903 to 927 and its continued use of Buddhist kingship.

sources.title: Buddhist kingship and governance in the Dali kingdom
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Journal of Southeast Asian Studies article used for Dali governance, major clans, the Dazhong interruption, imported books, medical texts and Buddhist statecraft.

sources.title: University of Pittsburgh: Buddhism and visual culture in the Dali kingdom
sources.note: University dissertation used narrowly for Dali’s 937 to 1253 span and the brief Dazhong interruption from 1094 to 1096 before Later Dali.

sources.title: The Annan Protectorate during the Tang period
sources.note: Peer-reviewed regional history used narrowly for Nanzhao’s occupation of Annan from 863 to 866, its garrison and the Tang reconquest.

sources.title: Horses, silver, and cowries: Yunnan in global perspective
sources.note: Peer-reviewed Journal of World History publication record and abstract used for horse trade, silver exports, cowry money and Yunnan’s links across East, Southeast and Inner Asia.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Twenty-four-armed Avalokiteshvara
sources.note: Museum object record for a gilt arsenical-bronze Dali sculpture dated to the eleventh or twelfth century, including its protective tantric form and held attributes.

sources.title: National Palace Museum: Long Scroll of Buddhist Images
sources.note: Museum record for Zhang Shengwen’s Dali scroll, its 1172 to 1175 colophon, imperial offering scene, hundreds of figures and Buddhist texts written in Chinese and Sanskrit.

sources.title: Smithsonian: Illustrated Sutra of the Deeds of the Buddha documentation
sources.note: Museum documentation for a twelfth- or thirteenth-century Dali handscroll, married donors Chen Qing and Lian, and a Yunnanese father-son naming link.

sources.title: Oxford Research Encyclopedia: The Sino-Tibetan borderlands
sources.note: Scholarly regional synthesis used for the Dali kingdom’s 937 to 1253 span, the Mongol campaign and the start of longer political integration into imperial China.

sources.title: From Kingdom to Frontier: Yunnan under Mongol-Yuan and Ming rule
sources.note: University of California dissertation abstract used for the 1253 conquest and the Mongol-Yuan use of Dali personnel, institutions and religious-political traditions after conquest.

proposedOverrides.summary: An atlas label spans historical Nanzhao, short successor regimes, Dali and Mongol rule; Erhai communities continued as dynasties and borders changed.

batchIdentityNotes: The exact id nan-chao is indexed circa 800 to 1279 as a state and had no tracked card or override before integration.

At 800 and 900 the feature is one 20- or 21-position Polygon that excludes Taihe, Dali and Weishan while including Kunming and Luang Prabang. Both early geometries are seriously misplaced southeast of the historical Nanzhao core.

At 1000 the polygon shifts west and includes Dali, Weishan and Kunming. The 1100 and 1200 versions keep that general successor-era footprint, but historical Nanzhao had already ended in 902 and Dali had begun in 937.
The separate nan-zhao predecessor id remains distinct. No appliesTo alias is used, and its already documented world-700 geometry problem is not silently transferred to this target.

The id is absent at the 700 predecessor seam and 1279 ending seam. Its 1279 endpoint is atlas coverage, while the override records 902 as the historical Nanzhao fall and the card narrates Dali’s 1253 conquest separately.
All bounds, hashes and point tests describe imported display geometry only; none establishes ethnic identity, spoken language, precise political control or modern territorial claims.
